nameStory: This starfish gets its "purple" name from the beautiful violet to deep purple coloration that often decorates its arms and central disc. The "sun star" part comes from its distinctive radiating arms that spread out like sun rays - typically 9-11 arms compared to the usual 5 arms of most starfish. "Smooth" refers to its relatively even surface texture compared to other bumpy or spiny sea stars.
description: The Purple Sun Star is a large, multi-armed starfish found in New England's cold coastal waters. Unlike the familiar 5-armed starfish, this impressive creature typically has 9-11 arms radiating from a central disc, creating a sun-like appearance. It can grow quite large, often reaching 8-16 inches across when fully extended. The coloration ranges from purple and violet to reddish-orange or brown, often with contrasting lighter or darker patterns on the arms.

idTips.label: Arm Count
idTips.description: Count 9-11 arms radiating from the center - this immediately sets it apart from most 5-armed starfish you'll encounter

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Look for purple, violet, or reddish hues, often with lighter patches or bands across the arms that create striking contrast

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large and impressive - often spans 8-16 inches across, making it one of the bigger starfish in New England waters

idTips.label: Arm Shape
idTips.description: Arms are relatively thick at the base and taper gradually to pointed tips, feeling firm and substantial when gently touched

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Skin feels smooth to slightly rough, not covered in obvious spines or bumps like some other large starfish

idTips.label: Central Disc
idTips.description: The center body is proportionally large compared to the arms, giving it a robust, well-fed appearance

habitat: Purple Sun Stars live in cold New England waters, typically found in deeper areas from the low tide zone down to considerable depths. They prefer rocky bottoms, kelp beds, and areas with good water circulation along the Maine coast and occasionally Massachusetts waters. Look for them in tide pools during very low tides, or while snorkeling in deeper rocky areas where they hunt for other sea stars and marine invertebrates.

seasonality.spring: More likely to be found in accessible tide pools as winter storms subside and extremely low tides expose deeper areas. This is when they may be closer to shore.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for spotting them during low tides or while exploring tide pools. Warmer weather makes tide pooling more comfortable, though they prefer the cooler waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active and visible during low tides. Fall storms may occasionally wash specimens into shallower areas where they're easier to observe.
seasonality.winter: Generally in deeper water and less accessible to casual observers. Very hardy and active year-round in New England's cold waters.

funFact: Purple Sun Stars are actually cannibalistic predators that specialize in hunting and eating other starfish - they can smell their prey from a distance and will relentlessly pursue other sea stars, often appearing to "chase" them across the ocean floor in slow-motion underwater hunts!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other large starfish, but the 9-11 arms (instead of 5) are a dead giveaway. If you're counting arms and get more than 7, you're likely looking at a sun star species rather than a common sea star.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "starfish," these are actually echinoderms more closely related to sea urchins and sand dollars than to fish. The name "sun star" is used for several species in this family, so arm count and color are important for distinguishing the Purple Sun Star from its relatives.
compareHints: Since this is the only Solaster species commonly found in New England, compare it to other sun stars in the Solasteridae family. Purple Sun Stars typically have more arms (9-11) than many of their relatives and show the characteristic purple coloration. Other sun stars in the region may have different arm counts or lack the distinctive purple hues, often appearing more orange or red instead.
